Logit decay for correct tokens occurs under conflicting contexts, most pronounced in final layers.
Norm dynamics vary by architecture; Llama-3.1-8B shows dilution, but Qwen-3-4B and GLM-4-9B maintain stable norms.
Interference vectors are quasi-orthogonal to truth directions, supporting the orthogonal interference hypothesis.
Angular deviation correlates strongly with performance drop, indicating geometric rotation is the dominant mechanism.
Compliance is characterized by simulated adoption, where internal truth is bypassed, not erased.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, assuming truth and context interact as linear vectors.
Dataset scope restricted to fact-based QA tasks (MMLU), may not generalize to other tasks.
Focus on final residual state before unembedding, not layer-wise evolution of interference vectors.
Sample size of three architectures may not capture behaviors of larger or MoE models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently prioritize conflicting in-context information over pre-existing parametric memory, a phenomenon often termed sycophancy or compliance. However, the mechanistic realization of this behavior remains obscure, specifically how the model resolves these knowledge conflicts through compliance, and whether this suppression arises from signal magnitude dilution or directional geometric alteration within the residual stream. To resolve this, we conducted a layer-wise geometric analysis across Qwen-3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, and GLM-4-9B, decomposing the residual stream updates induced by counter-factual contexts into radial (norm-based) and angular (cosine-based) components. Our empirical results reject the universality of the "Manifold Dilution" hypothesis, as two of the three architectures maintained stable residual norms despite exhibiting significant performance degradation on factual queries. Instead, we observed that compliance is consistently characterized by "Orthogonal Interference," where the conflicting context injects a steering vector that is quasi-orthogonal to the ground-truth direction, effectively rotating the hidden state representation. This suggests that models do not "unlearn" or suppress the magnitude of internal truths but rather employ a mechanism of geometric displacement to bypass the correct unembedding vector, effectively simulating adoption while preserving the original structural magnitude. These findings challenge scalar confidence metrics for detecting hallucinations and underscore the necessity of vectorial monitoring to distinguish between genuine knowledge integration and superficial in-context mimicry.

papers.title: No Answer Needed: Predicting LLM Answer Accuracy from Question-Only Linear Probes
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) anticipate when they will answer correctly?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that a simple linear probe on residual stream activations can predict an LLM's forthcoming answer correctness, revealing a linearly separable 'factual correctness' signal that generalizes across knowledge domains but fails for mathematical reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The analysis advances understanding of how LLMs encode self-assessment, providing evidence for a general 'Factual Correctness' direction while highlighting the structural distinctness of reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
A correctness signal is linearly separable in the activation space and generalizes from trivia questions to other factual knowledge datasets.
The correctness direction fails to generalize to mathematical reasoning tasks (GSM8K), indicating a structural misalignment between factual and arithmetic correctness.
Linear separability of correctness is low in early layers and saturates at intermediate transformer layers.
For models that answer 'I don't know', doing so strongly correlates with the probe score, suggesting the same direction captures implicit confidence.
The in-advance correctness signal is strongest and most consistent for the largest model tested (Llama 3.3 70B).
papers.limitation: The learned correctness direction does not generalize to arithmetic-reasoning tasks (GSM8K).
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) anticipate when they will answer correctly? To study this, we extract activations after a question is read but before any tokens are generated, and train linear probes to predict whether the model's forthcoming answer will be correct. Across three open-source model families ranging from 7 to 70 billion parameters, projections on this "in-advance correctness direction" trained on generic trivia questions predict success in distribution and on diverse out-of-distribution knowledge datasets, indicating a deeper signal than dataset-specific spurious features, and outperforming black-box baselines and verbalised predicted confidence. Predictive power saturates in intermediate layers and, notably, generalisation falters on questions requiring mathematical reasoning. Moreover, for models responding "I don't know", doing so strongly correlates with the probe score, indicating that the same direction also captures confidence. By complementing previous results on truthfulness and other behaviours obtained with probes and sparse auto-encoders, our work contributes essential findings to elucidate LLM internals.

papers.title: Understanding Addition and Subtraction in Transformers
papers.research_question: Can transformers learn exact arithmetic algorithms for addition and subtraction, and how do they implement these algorithms?
papers.core_contribution: Small transformers can learn exact addition and subtraction algorithms with near-perfect accuracy, and these algorithms are implemented via interpretable circuits in attention heads and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can implement exact n-digit addition and subtraction through interpretable circuits, and with appropriate training, larger LLMs could in principle adopt the same mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Small transformers (2-3 layers, 3-4 heads) achieve >99.999% accuracy on n-digit addition and subtraction.
The models implement specific algorithms for addition and subtraction based on cascading carry and borrow circuits.
Mixed models initialized with addition weights can reuse circuits for subtraction, with many nodes becoming polysemantic.
Only 7% of 180 surveyed public LLMs can reliably perform addition without external tools.
The algorithmic implementation is consistent across seeds and model sizes, with attention heads and MLPs satisfying strict constraints.
papers.limitation:
The analysis does not examine the specific data representations and transformations used by polysemantic nodes, SGN nodes, and OPR nodes in the residual stream, nor the detailed mechanisms of MLP layers.
The automated framework for discovering algorithm subtasks has limitations and some aspects are specific to the math models studied.
Fully reverse engineering neural networks is challenging due to distributed parallel computations difficult to trace to specific components.
future_direction: Refine the declarative language for describing algorithms and the framework for testing these descriptions against models.
Further work to understand how identified components actually encode and manipulate information.
Investigate the universality of representations and circuits across models using the provided models.
papers.abstract: Transformers are widely deployed in large language models (LLMs), yet most models still fail on basic arithmetic tasks such as multidigit addition. In contrast, we show that small transformers trained from scratch can solve n-digit addition and subtraction with 99.999% accuracy. Building directly on prior work that uncovered addition circuits, we extend the analysis to subtraction and present a unified mechanistic account based on cascading carry and borrow circuits. Using a suite of 49 trained models, we apply systematic ablations and node-level constraints to validate the learned mechanisms and release a reproducible interpretability toolkit for studying arithmetic circuits. Finally, surveying 180 publicly available LLMs, we find that only 7% can reliably perform addition, underscoring the gap between specialized small models and general-purpose LLMs. Our results show that arithmetic can be implemented exactly by tiny transformers, offering a tractable case study for mechanistic interpretability and a cautionary contrast with the persistent arithmetic failures of much larger models.

papers.title: Under the Hood: Using Diagnostic Classifiers to Investigate and Improve\n how Language Models Track Agreement Information
papers.research_question: How do neural language models keep track of number agreement between subject and verb, and can diagnostic classifiers be used to understand and improve this ability?
papers.core_contribution: Diagnostic classifiers provide a detailed understanding of how, when, and where number agreement information is represented in an LSTM language model, and this knowledge can be used to improve model performance via targeted interventions on internal activations.
papers.conclusion: Diagnostic classifiers offer a detailed understanding of where and when information is encoded in a neural model, and this information can be used post hoc to actively influence the model's processing and improve its performance.
papers.key_findings:
Number information is best represented in the second layer of the LSTM, particularly in the hidden activation and memory cell.
Number information is represented dynamically over time, with a 'surface' level representation at the subject and verb timesteps and a more stable 'deep' representation in between.
For sentences where the model makes agreement errors, the number information is already corrupted at the subject timestep, before the attractor appears.
Intervening on the hidden and memory cell activations at the subject timestep using a diagnostic classifier significantly improves the model's agreement accuracy.
Diagnostic classifiers trained on different timesteps show that representations of number information are not uniform across time, as classifiers do not generalize well between subject/verb timesteps and intermediate timesteps.
papers.abstract:
How do neural language models keep track of number agreement between subject
and verb? We show that `diagnostic classifiers', trained to predict number from
the internal states of a language model, provide a detailed understanding of
how, when, and where this information is represented. Moreover, they give us
insight into when and where number information is corrupted in cases where the
language model ends up making agreement errors. To demonstrate the causal role
played by the representations we find, we then use agreement information to
influence the course of the LSTM during the processing of difficult sentences.
Results from such an intervention reveal a large increase in the language
model's accuracy. Together, these results show that diagnostic classifiers give
us an unrivalled detailed look into the representation of linguistic
information in neural models, and demonstrate that this knowledge can be used
to improve their performance.

papers.title: Language Models Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring and Control of Their Internal Activations
papers.research_question: Can LLMs accurately monitor and control their internal neural activations? Why can they report some intermediate steps but not others?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neurofeedback paradigm to quantify metacognitive abilities in LLMs, showing they can report and control internal activations along certain axes, with performance depending on interpretability, variance, and context.
papers.conclusion: LLMs have limited metacognitive abilities to monitor and control their internal activations, which raises important considerations for AI safety and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can report neural activations along target axes, with performance improving with more in-context examples and being better for semantically interpretable axes.
LLMs can explicitly and implicitly control neural activations, with explicit control being stronger and effects increasing with model size and depth.
Control effects are stronger for axes with semantic interpretability and those explaining more variance.
The axes that can be reported and controlled span a low-dimensional 'metacognitive space'.
Metacognitive abilities have implications for AI safety, as models might evade neural-based oversight.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to instruction-fine-tuned models and may not generalize to base models.
The neurofeedback paradigm assumes the model can understand the task, which may not hold for all models or tasks.
future_direction: Extend the neurofeedback paradigm to more models and datasets.
Investigate the neural mechanisms underlying metacognitive control in LLMs.
Explore applications in AI safety, such as developing better oversight methods.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can sometimes report the strategies they actually use to solve tasks, yet at other times seem unable to recognize those strategies that govern their behavior. This suggests a limited degree of metacognition - the capacity to monitor one's own cognitive processes for subsequent reporting and self-control. Metacognition enhances LLMs' capabilities in solving complex tasks but also raises safety concerns, as models may obfuscate their internal processes to evade neural-activation-based oversight (e.g., safety detector). Given society's increased reliance on these models, it is critical that we understand their metacognitive abilities. To address this, we introduce a neuroscience-inspired neurofeedback paradigm that uses in-context learning to quantify metacognitive abilities of LLMs to report and control their activation patterns. We demonstrate that their abilities depend on several factors: the number of in-context examples provided, the semantic interpretability of the neural activation direction (to be reported/controlled), and the variance explained by that direction. These directions span a "metacognitive space" with dimensionality much lower than the model's neural space, suggesting LLMs can monitor only a small subset of their neural activations. Our paradigm provides empirical evidence to quantify metacognition in LLMs, with significant implications for AI safety (e.g., adversarial attack and defense).

papers.title: Emergent effects of scaling on the functional hierarchies within large language models
papers.research_question: What is the functional hierarchy of abstraction across layers in LLMs, and how does it change with model scaling?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models exhibit functional hierarchies with abstraction increasing across layers, but scaling introduces deviations such as double representation peaks and anti-persistent fluctuations in attention mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms functional hierarchies in LLMs but reveals emergent deviations with scaling, such as double representation peaks and layer coordination, complicating interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Item-level semantics are most strongly represented in early layers (2-7), two-item relations in middle layers (8-12), and four-item analogies in later layers (10-15), consistent with an abstraction hierarchy.
Deep layers can represent narrow two-item relations from early in the context, suggesting information compression without meaningful abstraction.
In the large Llama-3.3-70b-Instruct model, representation of two-item relations and analogies shows two distinct peaks (layers 12-16 and 25-33), indicating fluctuations in abstraction level.
Adjacent layers in the large model exhibit anti-persistent fluctuations in attention outputs, with negative autocorrelation, suggesting coordinated specialization.
Buried concepts (target text followed by filler) are represented in deeper layers, showing that late layers capture global document-wide information.
papers.limitation:
The interpretation of the double-peak pattern and valley in large models is unclear and requires further work.
Analyses on grammar and syntax were inconclusive and not reported, limiting insights into syntactic processing.
future_direction: Study larger models to understand scaling effects further.
Investigate the mechanisms behind the double-peak representation and layer coordination.
Explore how late-layer representations can be used for steering and safety applications.
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) architectures are often described as functionally hierarchical: Early layers process syntax, middle layers begin to parse semantics, and late layers integrate information. The present work revisits these ideas. This research submits simple texts to an LLM (e.g., "A church and organ") and extracts the resulting activations. Then, for each layer, support vector machines and ridge regressions are fit to predict a text's label and thus examine whether a given layer encodes some information. Analyses using a small model (Llama-3.2-3b; 28 layers) partly bolster the common hierarchical perspective: Item-level semantics are most strongly represented early (layers 2-7), then two-item relations (layers 8-12), and then four-item analogies (layers 10-15). Afterward, the representation of items and simple relations gradually decreases in deeper layers that focus on more global information. However, several findings run counter to a steady hierarchy view: First, although deep layers can represent document-wide abstractions, deep layers also compress information from early portions of the context window without meaningful abstraction. Second, when examining a larger model (Llama-3.3-70b-Instruct), stark fluctuations in abstraction level appear: As depth increases, two-item relations and four-item analogies initially increase in their representation, then markedly decrease, and afterward increase again momentarily. This peculiar pattern consistently emerges across several experiments. Third, another emergent effect of scaling is coordination between the attention mechanisms of adjacent layers. Across multiple experiments using the larger model, adjacent layers fluctuate between what information they each specialize in representing. In sum, an abstraction hierarchy often manifests across layers, but large models also deviate from this structure in curious ways.

papers.title: Exploring Concept Depth: How Large Language Models Acquire Knowledge and Concept at Different Layers?
papers.research_question: Can shallow layers in LLMs capture meaningful features of simple knowledge, while complex concepts need deeper layers to capture their meaningful features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'Concept Depth' to measure how different layers in LLMs capture concepts of varying complexity, showing that simpler concepts are learned in shallow layers while complex concepts require deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Depth metric provides a useful framework for understanding how LLMs process concepts of varying complexity across layers, and the experimental insights enhance the understanding of internal representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler concepts (e.g., factual knowledge) are learned in shallow layers, while more complex concepts (e.g., reasoning tasks) require deeper layers for accurate understanding.
The pattern of Concept Depth is consistent across different model families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) and model sizes.
Larger models within a family tend to achieve higher peak accuracy and sometimes converge to optimal performance at earlier layers.
Adding noise to the input or quantizing model weights (e.g., to 8-bit) slows down the convergence of concept understanding, requiring deeper layers to achieve comparable accuracy.
Compressing models to 16-bit quantization does not significantly harm the understanding process compared to 32-bit.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performances across a wide range of tasks. However, the mechanisms by which these models encode tasks of varying complexities remain poorly understood. In this paper, we explore the hypothesis that LLMs process concepts of varying complexities in different layers, introducing the idea of "Concept Depth" to suggest that more complex concepts are typically acquired in deeper layers. Specifically, we categorize concepts based on their level of abstraction, defining them in the order of increasing complexity within factual, emotional, and inferential tasks. We conduct extensive probing experiments using layer-wise representations across various LLM families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) on various datasets spanning the three domains of tasks. Our findings reveal that models could efficiently conduct probing for simpler tasks in shallow layers, and more complex tasks typically necessitate deeper layers for accurate understanding. Additionally, we examine how external factors, such as adding noise to the input and quantizing the model weights, might affect layer-wise representations. Our findings suggest that these factors can impede the development of a conceptual understanding of LLMs until deeper layers are explored. We hope that our proposed concept and experimental insights will enhance the understanding of the mechanisms underlying LLMs. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Luckfort/CD.

papers.title: Diagnostic Classifiers: Revealing how Neural Networks Process Hierarchical Structure
papers.research_question: How do neural networks process hierarchical structure, and what strategies do they use for compositional semantics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces diagnostic classifiers as a method to test hypotheses about the strategies neural networks use, and shows that a GRU follows an incremental strategy for processing hierarchical arithmetic expressions.
papers.conclusion: Diagnostic classifiers are a useful method for understanding how neural networks process hierarchical structure, and the GRU follows an incremental strategy for the arithmetic task.
papers.key_findings:
TreeRNNs can learn to compute the meaning of arithmetic expressions and generalize to longer expressions.
The TreeRNN solution can be understood geometrically through projection, summation, and squashing steps.
GRUs can also learn the task and generalize to longer expressions, but performance deteriorates with length and is worse for right-branching expressions.
Diagnostic classifiers reveal that the GRU follows an incremental strategy rather than a recursive one.
The diagnostic classifier method is a useful tool for analyzing neural network internal dynamics when visualization is insufficient.
papers.limitation:
The TreeRNN requires external parses and is not computationally efficient or biologically plausible.
The GRU's performance deteriorates with sentence length and is worse for right-branching sentences.
The diagnostic classifiers are linear and may not capture all information; the predictions change at every time step while target values remain the same, indicating a possible refinement.
papers.abstract: We investigate how neural networks can be used for hierarchical, compositional semantics. To this end, we define the simple but nontrivial artificial task of processing nested arithmetic expressions and study whether different types of neural networks can learn to add and subtract. We find that recursive neural networks can implement a generalising solution, and we visualise the intermediate steps: projection, summation and squashing. We also show that gated recurrent neural networks, which process the expressions incrementally, perform surprisingly well on this task: they learn to predict the outcome of the arithmetic expressions with reasonable accuracy, although performance deteriorates with increasing length. To analyse what strategy the recurrent network applies, visualisation techniques are less insightful. Therefore, we develop an approach where we formulate and test hypotheses on what strategies these networks might be following. For each hypothesis, we derive predictions about features of the hidden state representations at each time step, and train ’diagnostic classifiers’ to test those predictions. Our results indicate the networks follow a strategy similar to our hypothesised ’incremental strategy’.

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual transformers like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate layers representing concepts in English before mapping to the target language, indicating an English bias in their internal representations.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs have an English bias in their internal representations, which may lead to linguistic biases and has implications for equitable AI.
papers.key_findings:
In translation tasks, intermediate layers decode the English version of the correct next token before switching to the target language.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space, concept space (biased towards English), and output space.
Token energy is low in middle layers, indicating that latents are in a concept space orthogonal to token space.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The same pattern is observed in Mistral-7B, suggesting generality of the phenomenon.
papers.limitation:
Focus on Llama-2 family, so claims may not generalize to other models.
Tasks are simple and controlled, not real-world.
Limited understanding of the concept space structure.
Logit lens only reveals part of the internal state.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias affects downstream model behavior.
Study how English bias changes with different training data or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks and models.

papers.title: Understanding the Countably Infinite: Neural Network Models of the Successor Function and its Acquisition
papers.research_question: How do children learn the successor function, what latent number representations make this possible, and what does it mean to understand the countably infinite?
papers.core_contribution: The place-value model shows a drop in representational similarity across tens boundaries, revealing that counting across a tens boundary can be understood as a vector operation in 2D space, and curriculum learning shows sharpening of smaller number representations during development.
papers.conclusion: This study is a first step in using neural networks to understand the successor function, and future work should explore recurrent architectures for modeling the counting process more generally.
papers.key_findings:
The count list model achieved perfect training accuracy but 0% test accuracy, indicating no generalization.
The place-value model showed 24% test accuracy and sensitivity to tens boundaries in representational similarity.
MDS analysis revealed systematic mapping of numbers to successors across tens boundaries in the place-value model.
Curriculum learning simulations showed incremental learning and sharpening of representations for smaller numbers.
The models did not learn the successor function well for the highest test range (81-99) in curriculum learning.
papers.limitation:
The count list model lacks sensitivity to tens boundaries, which is critical for place-value structure.
The place-value model has low test accuracy (24%) and does not generalize perfectly.
The models learn formally different ML tasks, making direct comparison difficult.
In curriculum learning, the highest test range (81-99) was not learned well even with additional training.
future_direction: Move beyond generating the successor of a number to modeling the counting process more generally.
Explore training recurrent neural network models to sequentially count, first to 100 and then arbitrarily high.
Use richer recurrent architectures to learn the recursive structure of natural numbers.
papers.abstract: As children enter elementary school, their understanding of the ordinal structure of numbers transitions from a memorized count list of the first 50-100 numbers to knowing the successor function and understanding the countably infinite. We investigate this developmental change in two neural network models that learn the successor function on the pairs (N, N+1) for N in (0, 98). The first uses a one-hot encoding of the input and output values and corresponds to children memorizing a count list, while the second model uses a place-value encoding and corresponds to children learning the language rules for naming numbers. The place-value model showed a predicted drop in representational similarity across tens boundaries. Counting across a tens boundary can be understood as a vector operation in 2D space, where the numbers with the same tens place are organized in a linearly separable manner, whereas those with the same ones place are grouped together. A curriculum learning simulation shows that, in the expanding numerical environment of the developing child, representations of smaller numbers continue to be sharpened even as larger numbers begin to be learned. These models set the stage for future work using recurrent architectures to move beyond learning the successor function to simulating the counting process more generally, and point towards a deeper understanding of what it means to understand the countably infinite.

papers.title: Learning Inductive Biases with Simple Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do simple neural networks develop inductive biases like the shape bias, and under what conditions? How does the acquisition of this bias relate to vocabulary acceleration, mirroring child development?
papers.core_contribution: Simple neural networks can learn a shape bias from very few examples, and the development of this bias predicts vocabulary acceleration in the networks, consistent with developmental processes in children.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can learn inductive biases like the shape bias from limited data, and the dynamics of this learning mirror child development, suggesting a connection between artificial and human learning.
papers.key_findings:
Multilayer perceptrons develop a shape bias after seeing as few as 3 examples of 4 object categories using abstract bit-vector patterns.
Convolutional neural networks develop a shape bias with as few as 6 examples of 8 object categories using synthetic images.
Networks show greater sensitivity to changes in shape than color after shape bias training, as shown by parametric manipulation of stimuli.
The development of the shape bias in CNNs correlates with the onset of vocabulary acceleration, mirroring the correlation observed in children.
Color bias training requires less data than shape bias training and does not follow the same two-step generalization process.
future_direction: Investigate the hypothesis of initializing large-scale image recognition models with shape bias training using ImageNet-scale DNNs.
papers.abstract: People use rich prior knowledge about the world in order to efficiently learn new concepts. These priors - also known as "inductive biases" - pertain to the space of internal models considered by a learner, and they help the learner make inferences that go beyond the observed data. A recent study found that deep neural networks optimized for object recognition develop the shape bias (Ritter et al., 2017), an inductive bias possessed by children that plays an important role in early word learning. However, these networks use unrealistically large quantities of training data, and the conditions required for these biases to develop are not well understood. Moreover, it is unclear how the learning dynamics of these networks relate to developmental processes in childhood. We investigate the development and influence of the shape bias in neural networks using controlled datasets of abstract patterns and synthetic images, allowing us to systematically vary the quantity and form of the experience provided to the learning algorithms. We find that simple neural networks develop a shape bias after seeing as few as 3 examples of 4 object categories. The development of these biases predicts the onset of vocabulary acceleration in our networks, consistent with the developmental process in children.

papers.title: How Large Language Models Encode Context Knowledge? A Layer-Wise Probing Study
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode context knowledge across different layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a layer-wise probing framework to study how LLMs encode context knowledge, finding that more context knowledge is encoded in upper layers and that knowledge-related entity tokens encode knowledge earlier, with knowledge spreading to other tokens via attention.
papers.conclusion: Proposes a novel layer-wise probing framework for explaining how LLMs encode context knowledge, demonstrating that LLMs encode more knowledge in upper layers and transfer knowledge from entity tokens to other tokens, with retention diminishing with irrelevant evidence.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers.
LLMs primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers.
LLMs gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence.
Base models have lower capability to encode knowledge through prompting compared to chat models.
The long-term memory capability of LLMs degrades when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical mechanism behind the observed phenomena remains an open issue.
Experiments are limited to LLaMA 2 models, ignoring other SOTA models.
future_direction: Mathematical understanding of the role of self-attention in knowledge transfer.
Experiments on more PLMs (e.g., PaLM, OPT, Pythia).
papers.abstract: Previous work has showcased the intriguing capability of large language models (LLMs) in retrieving facts and processing context knowledge. However, only limited research exists on the layer-wise capability of LLMs to encode knowledge, which challenges our understanding of their internal mechanisms. In this paper, we devote the first attempt to investigate the layer-wise capability of LLMs through probing tasks. We leverage the powerful generative capability of ChatGPT to construct probing datasets, providing diverse and coherent evidence corresponding to various facts. We employ $\mathcal V$-usable information as the validation metric to better reflect the capability in encoding context knowledge across different layers. Our experiments on conflicting and newly acquired knowledge show that LLMs: (1) prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers; (2) primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers; and (3) gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Jometeorie/probing_llama.

papers.title: Signatures of human-like processing in Transformer forward passes
papers.research_question: Do Transformer forward passes show mechanistic signatures of human-like processing, such as competitor interference? Do dynamic measures from forward passes improve prediction of human processing indicators compared to static output measures? How does model size affect the similarity between model and human processing?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer forward passes show signatures of human-like competitor interference and two-stage processing. Dynamic measures from layer-wise computations improve the prediction of human processing indicators compared to static output measures.
papers.conclusion: The work suggests a new way of using AI models to study human cognition: not just as black boxes mapping stimuli to responses, but potentially also as explicit processing models whose internal dynamics resemble human cognitive processing.
papers.key_findings:
LMs show signs of competitor interference, with delayed decision-making and two-stage processing for items with salient intuitive answers.
Measures of layer-time dynamics (e.g., COM, TTD) improve the ability to predict human processing indicators (accuracy, response time, typing/mouse patterns) above and beyond static final-layer measures.
Larger models are not always most predictive of human processing; mid-size LMs show the strongest signs of two-stage processing.
The similarity between model and human processing appears to emerge through general-purpose objectives like next-token prediction or image recognition.
Results generalize across text and vision modalities and multiple model families.
papers.limitation: The logit lens method may be brittle, though results were qualitatively similar with the tuned lens.
future_direction: Extending the approach to more models, tasks, and modalities.
Investigating the relationship between model processing dynamics and other fine-grained human behavioral measures.
papers.abstract: Modern AI models are increasingly being used as theoretical tools to study human cognition. One dominant approach is to evaluate whether human-derived measures are predicted by a model's output: that is, the end-product of a forward pass. However, recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have begun to reveal the internal processes that give rise to model outputs, raising the question of whether models might use human-like processing strategies. Here, we investigate the relationship between real-time processing in humans and layer-time dynamics of computation in Transformers, testing 20 open-source models in 6 domains. We first explore whether forward passes show mechanistic signatures of competitor interference, taking high-level inspiration from cognitive theories. We find that models indeed appear to initially favor a competing incorrect answer in the cases where we would expect decision conflict in humans. We then systematically test whether forward-pass dynamics predict signatures of processing in humans, above and beyond properties of the model's output probability distribution. We find that dynamic measures improve prediction of human processing measures relative to static final-layer measures. Moreover, across our experiments, larger models do not always show more human-like processing patterns. Our work suggests a new way of using AI models to study human cognition: not just as a black box mapping stimuli to responses, but potentially also as explicit processing models.

papers.title: Learning to Trust Your Feelings: Leveraging Self-awareness in LLMs for Hallucination Mitigation
papers.research_question: How well can LLMs discern and express their internal knowledge state to mitigate factual hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLMs can discern their internal knowledge state with high accuracy but often fail to express it, leading to hallucinations. It introduces the RLKF training framework, which uses knowledge feedback via reinforcement learning to improve model factuality and honesty.
papers.conclusion: RLKF is effective in improving the model's utilization of its internal knowledge state, enhancing performance in knowledge and honesty related tasks, and is a promising solution for hallucination mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are highly adept at discerning their internal knowledge, with over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing.
DreamCatcher, an automatic hallucination detection tool, achieves 81% agreement with human annotators.
RLKF training enhances the factuality and honesty of LLMs, improving performance on knowledge-based tasks.
RLKF avoids the 'alignment tax' and improves benchmark performance on various tasks.
The reward model can quickly achieve high accuracy by utilizing internal knowledge state.
papers.abstract: We evaluate the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to discern and express their internal knowledge state, a key factor in countering factual hallucination and ensuring reliable application of LLMs. We observe a robust self-awareness of internal knowledge state in LLMs, evidenced by over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing. However, LLMs often fail to express their internal knowledge during generation, leading to factual hallucinations. We develop an automated hallucination annotation tool, Dreamcatcher, which merges knowledge probing and consistency checking methods to rank factual preference data. Using knowledge preference as reward, We propose a Reinforcement Learning from Knowledge Feedback (RLKF) training framework, leveraging reinforcement learning to enhance the factuality and honesty of LLMs. Our experiments across multiple models show that RLKF training effectively enhances the ability of models to utilize their internal knowledge state, boosting performance in a variety of knowledge-based and honesty-related tasks.

papers.title: Highway and Residual Networks learn Unrolled Iterative Estimation
papers.research_question: Does the traditional representation view adequately explain Highway and Residual networks? The paper proposes an alternative viewpoint based on unrolled iterative estimation.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the unrolled iterative estimation view as an alternative to the representation view for understanding Highway and Residual networks, showing that both architectures can be derived from this perspective and that it explains phenomena like resilience to lesioning and layer shuffling.
papers.conclusion: The paper offers a new perspective on Highway and Residual networks as performing unrolled iterative estimation, providing a unified theory and explaining recent findings, and hopes this perspective will guide future research.
papers.key_findings:
Highway and Residual networks perform unrolled iterative estimation, where blocks within a stage refine a single representation rather than computing new ones.
The mean estimation error in Residual networks is close to zero, supporting the iterative refinement view.
Visualization shows that filters refine their responses within a stage rather than changing feature type.
Highway and Residual networks perform similarly on image classification when gates are equally expressive.
For language modeling, gated variants (Highway) outperform non-gated (Residual) because dynamic feature replacement is beneficial.
future_direction: Further investigation into the unrolled iterative estimation perspective
Guiding research to understand, improve, and combine Highway and Residual networks
papers.abstract: The past year saw the introduction of new architectures such as Highway networks and Residual networks which, for the first time, enabled the training of feedforward networks with dozens to hundreds of layers using simple gradient descent. While depth of representation has been posited as a primary reason for their success, there are indications that these architectures defy a popular view of deep learning as a hierarchical computation of increasingly abstract features at each layer. In this report, we argue that this view is incomplete and does not adequately explain several recent findings. We propose an alternative viewpoint based on unrolled iterative estimation -- a group of successive layers iteratively refine their estimates of the same features instead of computing an entirely new representation. We demonstrate that this viewpoint directly leads to the construction of Highway and Residual networks. Finally we provide preliminary experiments to discuss the similarities and differences between the two architectures.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: Can LLMs Detect Their Confabulations? Estimating Reliability in Uncertainty-Aware Language Models
papers.research_question: How does in-context information influence model behavior and response uncertainty, and can uncertainty signals be used to predict response reliability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a context-controlled evaluation framework to study how context quality affects LLM responses, shows that token-level uncertainty can misalign with correctness under misleading context, and proposes a probing-based method using uncertainty-guided hidden state aggregation for improved reliability detection.
papers.conclusion: Providing accurate context improves model accuracy and confidence, while misleading context leads to confidently incorrect outputs, revealing a misalignment between uncertainty and correctness. The probing-based approach using uncertainty-guided hidden state aggregation improves reliability detection over uncertainty-only baselines.
papers.key_findings:
Correct context improves both answer accuracy and model confidence.
Misleading context often induces confidently incorrect responses.
Token-level uncertainty does not always align with correctness, particularly under misleading context.
Probing classifiers using aggregated hidden states from high-uncertainty tokens outperform direct uncertainty metrics for reliability detection.
Aggregating features from multiple tokens yields better performance than single-token features.
future_direction: Developing reliability-aware generation and context validation/filtering mechanisms for multi-turn or retrieval-augmented generation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are prone to generating fluent but incorrect content, known as confabulation, which poses increasing risks in multi-turn or agentic applications where outputs may be reused as context. In this work, we investigate how in-context information influences model behavior and whether LLMs can identify their unreliable responses. We propose a reliability estimation that leverages token-level uncertainty to guide the aggregation of internal model representations. Specifically, we compute aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty from output logits to identify salient tokens and aggregate their hidden states into compact representations for response-level reliability prediction. Through controlled experiments on open QA benchmarks, we find that correct in-context information improves both answer accuracy and model confidence, while misleading context often induces confidently incorrect responses, revealing a misalignment between uncertainty and correctness. Our probing-based method captures these shifts in model behavior and improves the detection of unreliable outputs across multiple open-source LLMs. These results underscore the limitations of direct uncertainty signals and highlight the potential of uncertainty-guided probing for reliability-aware generation.

papers.title: Massive Values in Self-Attention Modules are the Key to Contextual Knowledge Understanding
papers.research_question: What is the role of massive values in self-attention queries and keys, and how do they contribute to contextual knowledge understanding versus parametric knowledge retrieval?
papers.core_contribution: Massive values in attention queries and keys are critical for contextual knowledge understanding, and their concentration is caused by Rotary Positional Encoding (RoPE).
papers.conclusion: The findings shed new light on how queries and keys operate in LLMs and offer practical insights for model design and optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Massive values are concentrated in specific regions of attention queries and keys exclusively in models with RoPE.
These massive values are critical for contextual knowledge understanding rather than parametric knowledge retrieval.
Quantization methods that protect massive values preserve contextual understanding capabilities.
The concentration of massive values is caused by RoPE and appears from the first layers.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success in contextual knowledge understanding. In this paper, we show that these concentrated massive values consistently emerge in specific regions of attention queries (Q) and keys (K) while not having such patterns in values (V) in various modern transformer-based LLMs (Q, K, and V mean the representations output by the query, key, and value layers respectively). Through extensive experiments, we further demonstrate that these massive values play a critical role in interpreting contextual knowledge (knowledge obtained from the current context window) rather than in retrieving parametric knowledge stored within the model's parameters. Our further investigation of quantization strategies reveals that ignoring these massive values leads to a pronounced drop in performance on tasks requiring rich contextual understanding, aligning with our analysis. Finally, we trace the emergence of concentrated massive values and find that such concentration is caused by Rotary Positional Encoding (RoPE), which has appeared since the first layers. These findings shed new light on how Q and K operate in LLMs and offer practical insights for model design and optimization. The Code is Available at https://github.com/MingyuJ666/Rope_with_LLM.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: Language Models Fail to Introspect About Their Knowledge of Language
papers.research_question: Do large language models have the ability to introspect about their internal linguistic knowledge, specifically grammatical knowledge and word prediction?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs do not exhibit introspection about their linguistic knowledge; their metalinguistic responses are not more aligned with their own internal probabilities than with those of similar models.
papers.conclusion: LLMs cannot introspect about their linguistic knowledge, and metalinguistic prompting should not be conflated with models' internal linguistic generalizations.
papers.key_findings:
Models achieve high accuracy on grammaticality and word prediction tasks under both direct (probability-based) and metalinguistic (prompt-based) evaluation methods.
The consistency between direct and metalinguistic evaluations is low (Cohen’s κ around 0.25).
There is no evidence of introspection: within-model alignment between metalinguistic and direct evaluations is not higher than cross-model alignment when controlling for model similarity.
Model similarity (both feature-based and empirical) predicts the alignment between metalinguistic and direct evaluations, but there is no additional 'same model effect'.
Larger models tend to have better performance on metalinguistic prompts and their metalinguistic responses are more correlated with direct evaluations.
papers.limitation:
The study only tested open-source models; closed-source models might behave differently.
The null result might be due to the specific tasks and models; introspection might emerge in other settings.
papers.abstract: There has been recent interest in whether large language models (LLMs) can introspect about their own internal states. Such abilities would make LLMs more interpretable, and also validate the use of standard introspective methods in linguistics to evaluate grammatical knowledge in models (e.g., asking "Is this sentence grammatical?"). We systematically investigate emergent introspection across 21 open-source LLMs, in two domains where introspection is of theoretical interest: grammatical knowledge and word prediction. Crucially, in both domains, a model's internal linguistic knowledge can be theoretically grounded in direct measurements of string probability. We then evaluate whether models' responses to metalinguistic prompts faithfully reflect their internal knowledge. We propose a new measure of introspection: the degree to which a model's prompted responses predict its own string probabilities, beyond what would be predicted by another model with nearly identical internal knowledge. While both metalinguistic prompting and probability comparisons lead to high task accuracy, we do not find evidence that LLMs have privileged "self-access". By using general tasks, controlling for model similarity, and evaluating a wide range of open-source models, we show that LLMs cannot introspect, and add new evidence to the argument that prompted responses should not be conflated with models' linguistic generalizations.

papers.title: Fine-Tuned LLMs Know They Don't Know: A Parameter-Efficient Approach to Recovering Honesty
papers.research_question: Does honesty degradation in fine-tuned LLMs stem from a loss of self-knowledge or a failure of self-expression, and how can honesty be recovered efficiently?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes HCNR, a parameter-efficient method to recover honesty in fine-tuned LLMs by identifying and restoring honesty-critical neurons to their pre-trained states and applying Hessian-guided compensation.
papers.conclusion: HCNR provides an efficient, targeted solution for recovering honesty in fine-tuned LLMs by restoring critical neurons and compensating for misalignment, enabling trustworthy deployment in high-stakes domains.
papers.key_findings:
Honesty degradation in fine-tuned LLMs is a spurious phenomenon caused by impaired self-expression, not a loss of self-knowledge.
HCNR effectively recovers honesty (33.25% improvement) with minimal data (256 samples) and parameter changes (20%), achieving at least 2.23x speedup over baselines.
HCNR achieves a superior trade-off between downstream task performance and honesty compared to baseline methods like RAIT, DPO, and ORPO.
The method generalizes across different LLM families (Llama, Qwen, Mistral) and training paradigms (LoRA and full fine-tuning).
Ablation studies confirm the necessity of both stages: identifying honesty-critical neurons and applying Hessian-guided compensation.
papers.abstract: The honesty of Large Language Models (LLMs) is increasingly important for safe deployment in high-stakes domains. However, this crucial trait is severely undermined by supervised fine-tuning (SFT), a common technique for model specialization. Existing recovery methods rely on data-intensive global parameter adjustments, implicitly assuming that SFT deeply corrupts the models' ability to recognize their knowledge boundaries. However, we observe that fine-tuned LLMs still preserve this ability; what is damaged is their capacity to faithfully express that awareness. Building on this, we propose Honesty-Critical Neurons Restoration (HCNR) to surgically repair this suppressed capacity. HCNR identifies and restores key expression-governing neurons to their pre-trained state while harmonizing them with task-oriented neurons via Hessian-guided compensation. Experiments on four QA tasks and five LLM families demonstrate that HCNR effectively recovers 33.25% of the compromised honesty while achieving at least 2.23x speedup with over 10x less data compared to baseline methods, offering a practical solution for trustworthy LLM deployment.

papers.title: Visualisation and 'Diagnostic Classifiers' Reveal How Recurrent and Recursive Neural Networks Process Hierarchical Structure
papers.research_question: How do neural networks learn and process languages with hierarchical, compositional semantics, specifically whether they can compute the meaning of nested arithmetic expressions and how they do so.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces diagnostic classifiers as a method to analyze internal representations of recurrent neural networks and shows that GRUs follow a cumulative strategy for processing hierarchical arithmetic expressions.
papers.conclusion: Diagnostic classifiers can open the black box of neural networks and reveal the strategies they use, with GRUs approximating a cumulative strategy for processing hierarchical structure.
papers.key_findings:
TreeRNNs learn a recursive solution to compute arithmetic expressions and generalize to longer expressions.
GRUs can learn to compute arithmetic expressions and generalize, but performance deteriorates with length.
Diagnostic classifiers reveal that GRUs follow a strategy similar to a cumulative strategy, not a recursive strategy.
The method of diagnostic classifiers is proposed as a scalable way to analyze high-dimensional RNNs.
Visualization techniques like project-sum-squash provide insight into the TreeRNN's composition function.
papers.limitation:
Diagnostic classifiers for gates may require more complex architectures to handle non-linearities.
The analysis is on an idealized task and has not been applied to deeper networks and real-world tasks.
The network's strategy deviates from the perfect cumulative strategy, especially for right-branching expressions.
future_direction: Using diagnostic classifiers for gates with non-linear architectures.
Applying diagnostic classification to higher-dimensional networks and real-world tasks like language modeling and machine translation.
Further research into the reasons for the mismatch between the network's strategy and the cumulative strategy for right-branching expressions.
papers.abstract: We investigate how neural networks can learn and process languages with hierarchical, compositional semantics. To this end, we define the artificial task of processing nested arithmetic expressions, and study whether different types of neural networks can learn to compute their meaning. We find that recursive neural networks can implement a generalising solution to this problem, and we visualise this solution by breaking it up in three steps: project, sum and squash. As a next step, we investigate recurrent neural networks, and show that a gated recurrent unit, that processes its input incrementally, also performs very well on this task: the network learns to predict the outcome of the arithmetic expressions with high accuracy, although performance deteriorates somewhat with increasing length. To develop an understanding of what the recurrent network encodes, visualisation techniques alone do not suffice. Therefore, we develop an approach where we formulate and test multiple hypotheses on the information encoded and processed by the network. For each hypothesis, we derive predictions about features of the hidden state representations at each time step, and train 'diagnostic classifiers' to test those predictions. Our results indicate that the networks follow a strategy similar to our hypothesised 'cumulative strategy', which explains the high accuracy of the network on novel expressions, the generalisation to longer expressions than seen in training, and the mild deterioration with increasing length. This in turn shows that diagnostic classifiers can be a useful technique for opening up the black box of neural networks. We argue that diagnostic classification, unlike most visualisation techniques, does scale up from small networks in a toy domain, to larger and deeper recurrent networks dealing with real-life data, and may therefore contribute to a better understanding of the internal dynamics of current state-of-the-art models in natural language processing.

papers.title: How Pre-trained Word Representations Capture Commonsense Physical Comparisons
papers.research_question: Does pre-trained word representations capture commonsense physical comparisons between objects?
papers.core_contribution: Pre-trained word representations encode commonsense physical comparisons, and a simple probing model using these frozen embeddings achieves higher accuracy than previous methods and generalizes to unseen objects.
papers.conclusion: Pre-trained word representations encode physical commonsense comparisons, and a simple probing model can leverage this with high accuracy and generalization, learning an ordering over objects for comparisons.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained representations (GloVe, ELMo, BERT) capture physical commonsense comparisons with better accuracy than previous approaches.
The probing model generalizes to objects not seen during training, achieving higher accuracy on new datasets.
Models learn a consistent ordering over all objects involved in comparisons, using logit differences to form local orderings.
Linear probing models perform similarly to shallow neural networks, indicating that the embeddings themselves contain the necessary information.
The models struggle with ≈ comparisons due to class imbalance and the inherent difficulty of judging equality from an ordering.
papers.limitation: Models perform poorly on ≈ comparisons, likely due to class imbalance and the challenge of judging equality from learned orderings.
future_direction: Move beyond comparisons to directly probe for size estimates of physical properties for objects.
papers.abstract: Understanding common sense is important for effective natural language reasoning. One type of common sense is how two objects compare on physical properties such as size and weight: e.g., 'is a house bigger than a person?'. We probe whether pre-trained representations capture comparisons and find they, in fact, have higher accuracy than previous approaches. They also generalize to comparisons involving objects not seen during training. We investigate how such comparisons are made: models learn a consistent ordering over all the objects in the comparisons. Probing models have significantly higher accuracy than those baseline models which use dataset artifacts: e.g., memorizing some words are larger than any other word.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: Neural Correlates of Language Models Are Specific to Human Language
papers.research_question: Are correlations between language model hidden states and fMRI brain responses robust to dimensionality concerns, and are they specific to models trained on human language and dependent on positional encoding?
papers.core_contribution: The study confirms that correlations between transformer language model hidden states and human brain activity during language tasks are robust, specific to language-trained models, and heavily dependent on positional encodings.
papers.conclusion: The internal representations of transformer language models are strongly correlated with human brain activity during language processing, and this alignment is specific to language-trained models and relies on positional information.
papers.key_findings:
Removing positional encodings significantly reduces brain-model correlations and distorts the geometric similarity between model and brain representational spaces.
Dimensionality reduction via PCA does not eliminate the correlations, indicating they are not an artifact of the curse of dimensionality.
Models trained on non-linguistic data (protein sequences) show negligible alignment with brain activity, confirming the language-specificity of the effects.
Causal (decoder-only) language models show higher alignment with brain activity than bidirectional models.
The geometric structure of model and brain representations, measured by CKA and Gromov-Wasserstein distance, is similar and degrades when positional information is removed.
papers.limitation:
The dataset includes only 243 stimuli and 6 subjects, limiting statistical power and generalizability.
The head-wise analysis pooled voxels across cortical regions without distinguishing between different regions of interest.
The study uses text-only models and fMRI data from reading tasks; future work should use modality-matched datasets (e.g., audio models with spoken language tasks).
future_direction: Increase the number of subjects and model diversity to improve statistical power and generalizability.
Conduct finer-grained region-of-interest (ROI) by head analysis to reveal differential alignment patterns.
Use modality-matched datasets (e.g., spoken-language tasks with audio models) to disentangle task effects from representational differences.
papers.abstract: Previous work has shown correlations between the hidden states of large language models and fMRI brain responses, on language tasks. These correlations have been taken as evidence of the representational similarity of these models and brain states. This study tests whether these previous results are robust to several possible concerns. Specifically this study shows: (i) that the previous results are still found after dimensionality reduction, and thus are not attributable to the curse of dimensionality; (ii) that previous results are confirmed when using new measures of similarity; (iii) that correlations between brain representations and those from models are specific to models trained on human language; and (iv) that the results are dependent on the presence of positional encoding in the models. These results confirm and strengthen the results of previous research and contribute to the debate on the biological plausibility and interpretability of state-of-the-art large language models.

papers.title: Vision-Language Introspection: Mitigating Overconfident Hallucinations in MLLMs via Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering
papers.research_question: How to mitigate overconfident hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by simulating a metacognitive self-correction process that diagnoses and rectifies internal visual-semantic misalignments?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that mitigates object hallucinations in MLLMs by first introspectively localizing causal visual anchors and then performing interpretable bi-causal steering to rectify internal representations and calibrate overconfidence.
papers.conclusion: VLI effectively mitigates overconfident hallucinations in MLLMs by introspectively diagnosing visual-semantic conflicts and actively steering internal representations towards verified visual evidence, achieving state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
VLI reduces the object hallucination rate by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improves accuracy by up to 6.33% on POPE compared to baseline models.
Bi-causal steering, which isolates visual evidence from background noise via counterfactual representations, is the most critical component for error rectification.
The method successfully localizes interpretable visual anchors corresponding to high-risk tokens, enabling precise intervention.
VLI demonstrates robust generalization across diverse datasets (MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA) and model architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen3-VL).
Adaptive confidence calibration effectively penalizes ungrounded certainty, mitigating persistent hallucinations driven by blind confidence.
papers.limitation: The method introduces increased computational latency and memory overhead due to the parallel processing of counterfactual branches, though optimization reduces the impact.
papers.abstract: Object hallucination critically undermines the reliability of Multimodal Large Language Models, often stemming from a fundamental failure in cognitive introspection, where models blindly trust linguistic priors over specific visual evidence. Existing mitigations remain limited: contrastive decoding approaches operate superficially without rectifying internal semantic misalignments, while current latent steering methods rely on static vectors that lack instance-specific precision.
